subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

periods.activity_title: What Can Spin? Predicting and Listing
periods.textbook_anchor: How Things Work — Students make a list of objects they think can spin (p. 105)

time_bands.activity: Teacher tells the story of Meera and Dhruv watching a spinning coin and asks: 'Have you ever seen something spin and wondered how it keeps going?' Students share examples aloud.
Students open Textbook p. 105 and individually write a list of objects they think can spin. They then share with a partner and add any new objects their partner thought of.

Class builds a shared list on the board. Teacher guides students to sort the objects informally: 'Which of these have you actually seen spinning? Which are you guessing?' Discussion surfaces what students already know about spinning.

Students record their personal final list in their notebooks. Teacher poses a closing question: 'Do all objects spin the same way, or does something about their shape or size matter?' Students note one thought in response.

periods.implied_lo: Students can generate and refine predictions about which everyday objects are capable of a specified physical behaviour.
periods.section_context: Predicting and listing objects that can spin; sharing and comparing predictions with peers.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether the charkha — the spinning wheel that Gandhi used to spin cotton into thread — belongs on their list, and what makes it different from a coin or a top. This draws out what students already know about spinning tools without labelling it as a formal topic.

periods.textbook_anchor: How Things Work — Students collect and spin objects from the table and record observations (p. 105)

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes or asks students to collect the six objects: coin, bangle, pencil, stone, wooden top, eraser. Students open Textbook p. 105 and locate the observation table.

Students attempt to spin each object on their desk and observe: Does it spin? How long? Does it stay upright or topple? They record their findings in the table in their notebooks, using the textbook layout as a guide.
Groups of three compare their recorded observations. Where results differ, they attempt the spin again together and discuss why the outcome might have varied.
Teacher leads a quick whole-class share: 'Which objects surprised you? Did any object spin that you thought would not?' Students note one surprising finding.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the physical behaviour of a set of everyday objects under a common test condition.
periods.section_context: Spinning behaviour of coin, bangle, pencil, stone, wooden top (lattu), eraser.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students reach the wooden top (lattu), pause and ask whether anyone has played with a lattu or seen one used — this naturally surfaces knowledge of this traditional Indian spinning toy that has been in use for thousands of years. Keep the observation pace unhurried so every student records each object before moving to the next.

periods.textbook_anchor: How Things Work — Students make spinners from cardboard and toothpicks in different configurations and record observations (p. 106)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook pp. 106–108 and examine the spinner diagrams. Teacher demonstrates how to push a toothpick through the centre of a cardboard circle as the axle. Students identify the different spinner shapes shown.

Working in pairs, students make at least two spinner configurations — one with the axle at the centre and one with the axle off-centre. They spin each and record: Does it spin smoothly? For how long? Does it wobble?
Students share observations across pairs. Teacher asks: 'Where did you put the toothpick in the spinner that worked best?' The class identifies the centre-vs-off-centre difference together.
Students write one sentence in their notebooks: what they discovered about where the axle needs to be for a spinner to work well.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a hands-on investigation to test how changing the position of a component affects the physical behaviour of a self-made object.
periods.section_context: Cardboard spinners with toothpick axles; centre vs. off-centre axle position; spinner shape variation.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether the spinner they built resembles the lattu or the charkha in any way — what do all three have in common? This open question connects their constructed object to traditional spinning tools without interrupting the inquiry.

periods.activity_title: Why Did the Spinner Fail? Discussing Axle Position
periods.textbook_anchor: How Things Work — Students discuss which spinners did not spin properly and the role of hole position (p. 108)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure showing hole position comparison (p. 108)

time_bands.activity: Students bring out their spinners from earlier in this unit. They spin them again and sort them informally into 'spun well' and 'did not spin well'. They open Textbook p. 108 to the hole-position diagram.
In small groups, students discuss: 'Which spinners did not spin properly? What is different about them?' Groups record two possible reasons for poor spinning in their notebooks.

Whole-class discussion. Teacher uses the board to draw a spinner with centred hole vs. off-centre hole. Students explain in their own words why centring the axle matters. Teacher builds on their ideas to clarify the concept of balance in spinning.
Students revise one of their poorly-spinning spinners by adjusting the axle and test it. They note whether the change improved the spin.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain the effect of a structural variable on the performance of a simple physical device using evidence from their own tests.
periods.section_context: Spinner performance comparison; hole (axle) position at centre vs. off-centre; reasons for poor spinning.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Guide students to connect axle position to the idea of balance: 'If you carry a heavy bag on only one shoulder, what happens to your body?' This analogy from daily experience helps students articulate why off-centre placement causes wobble.

periods.activity_title: Colour Spinners: Mixing Colours Through Rotation
periods.textbook_anchor: How Things Work — Students colour spinners and observe colour-mixing effects during rotation (p. 106)
materials: Cardboard circles (pre-cut or cut in unit)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of coloured spinner segments (p. 106)

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'What do you think will happen if you colour different parts of a spinning disc in different colours and then spin it fast?' Students make a quick written prediction in their notebooks.

Each student colours a cardboard spinner disc in two or more distinct colour sections, then spins it. They observe what they see during fast rotation and record it in their notebooks alongside their original prediction.

Students compare predictions with outcomes in pairs. Teacher asks: 'Did the colours look the same spinning as they did still? What changed?' Students try different colour combinations and note whether the result changes.
Students write a brief observation statement: what colours they used, what they saw, and whether it matched their prediction.

periods.implied_lo: Students can make a prediction, carry out a test, and compare the outcome with their prediction to identify whether a physical phenomenon matched their expectation.
periods.section_context: Coloured cardboard spinner discs; colour-mixing effects during fast rotation; prediction vs. observation.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups whether they think the colour mixing they see is the same process used when a potter's wheel spins coloured clay — this open question invites students to connect the phenomenon to a familiar craft context.

periods.activity_title: Float or Sink? Predicting and Testing Objects
periods.textbook_anchor: Floating and Sinking — Students predict and observe float/sink behaviour of listed objects in water (p. 110)
materials: Bucket or large tub of water

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with the story from the textbook: Meera and Dhruv making paper boats after the rain. Students open Textbook p. 110 and locate the prediction-observation table. Teacher explains that students will first guess, then test.

In groups of four, students handle each object before placing it in the water, record their prediction (F or S), then drop it in and record the actual result. They work through all objects in Textbook p. 110.

Groups compare results across tables. Teacher asks: 'Which objects surprised you? Was the iron nail heavy or light? What about the empty bowl?' Students circle every result that did not match their prediction.
Students note one sentence: 'I was surprised that _____ because I thought _____.' This surfaces prior misconceptions for class discussion.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record predicted and observed outcomes for a physical test and identify where predictions and results diverge.
periods.section_context: Float/sink prediction and observation: leaf, iron nail, empty bowl (katori), plastic bottle with lid, pieces of stone, aluminium foil.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students reach the empty bowl, ask: 'Do fishermen in your area use boats made of heavy wood or metal? Does this surprise you?' This connects the phenomenon to real watercraft and opens the door to boat-making traditions.

periods.activity_title: Weight vs. Shape: Does Weight Alone Decide?
periods.textbook_anchor: Floating and Sinking — Students discuss whether all light objects float and all heavy objects sink (p. 111)
materials: Results table from this unit's observation activity

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 111 and re-examine their completed observation tables. Teacher poses the question from the textbook: 'Did all light objects float and all heavy objects sink?' Students mark 'Yes' or 'No' for each object.

Small-group discussion: students name the heavy objects that floated and the lighter objects that sank in their test. Groups try to explain why this happened. Teacher circulates and asks: 'What else is different about the empty bowl and the iron nail — besides weight?'
Whole-class sharing. Teacher records student reasoning on the board. Students begin to articulate that shape and how an object sits in water matters, not just how heavy it is.
Students write two sentences: one naming a heavy object that floated with a reason, and one naming a lighter object that sank with a reason.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use evidence from a physical test to challenge a simple rule and identify a factor other than the expected one that affects the outcome.
periods.section_context: Discussing whether weight alone determines floating or sinking; heavy objects that floated; lighter objects that sank.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether students have seen fishermen or their family members use bowls, gourds, or coconut shells on water — this surfaces traditional knowledge about materials used in water-based activities and keeps the discussion grounded in experience rather than abstraction.

periods.activity_title: Same Material, Different Shape: Aluminium Foil Investigation
periods.textbook_anchor: Floating and Sinking — Students test aluminium foil in three shapes and record float/sink results with reasons (p. 112)
materials: Aluminium foil (sufficient for three shapes per group)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 112. Teacher holds up a sheet of aluminium foil and asks: 'If I scrunch this into a ball and drop it in water, what will happen? What if I spread it flat? What if I fold it into a cup?' Students write quick predictions for all three shapes.

Working in pairs, students form three pieces of foil into: (1) spread flat, (2) pressed tightly into a ball, (3) folded into a cup shape. They test each in water, record F or S, and write a possible reason for each result in the Textbook p. 112 table format.
Pairs share results across groups. Teacher asks: 'The foil is the same material every time — so why does shape matter?' Students discuss what the cup shape traps compared with the ball shape.
Students complete a one-sentence conclusion: 'The shape of the foil changed whether it floated or sank because _____.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can investigate how changing the shape of the same material changes its physical behaviour in water and give a reason for the difference.
periods.section_context: Aluminium foil tested in three shapes: spread flat, pressed into a ball, folded into a cup; float or sink result and reasons for each shape.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: After students complete their test, ask: 'Traditional boats have been made from coconut shells and walnut shells — what shape are they, and does that match what you just found about shape and floating?' This connects the investigation finding to traditional boat forms without labelling it.

periods.activity_title: Design and Build: Our Classroom Boats
periods.textbook_anchor: Floating and Sinking — Students design, draw, and build boats from local materials and organise a classroom exhibition (p. 113)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook pp. 113–114. Teacher explains the task: each group of three to four students will design a boat, draw it first, build it, and then display it. Students form groups and discuss what materials they want to use.

Each group draws their boat design in their notebooks, labelling the materials. Teacher circulates and asks each group: 'How does your boat's shape connect to what you found out about floating?' Groups then begin building their boats using the available materials.
Groups test their boats in a tub of water. If a boat sinks, they adjust the design. Students complete the comparison table from Textbook p. 114: strengths and challenges of their boat.

Groups display their boats. A brief walk-around exhibition takes place: each group identifies one strength of another group's boat design. Students note the variety of designs achieved from the same set of materials.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use local materials to design, build, and evaluate a simple floating object, adjusting the design based on a test result.
periods.section_context: Boat design drawing; boat construction from paper, cardboard, ice-cream sticks, clay, adhesive tape; classroom exhibition; strengths and challenges comparison table.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: During the design stage, ask groups whether they have seen boats made from coconut shells or walnut shells — and whether that gives them any ideas for the shape of their own boat. This surfaces traditional material knowledge as a genuine design input.

periods.activity_title: Presenting Our Boat: Oral Findings and Reflection
periods.textbook_anchor: Floating and Sinking — Students compare boats and record strengths and challenges in the table (p. 114)

time_bands.activity: Each group prepares a short oral presentation (two to three sentences): what material they used, what shape they chose, and what happened when they tested it in water. Students refer to their design drawing and comparison table from their notebooks.
Groups present in turn. After each presentation, the class identifies one similarity and one difference between that group's boat and their own. Teacher notes recurring design decisions on the board.
Class discussion: 'Which shapes seemed to help boats float? Which materials worked best? Did any group change their design after testing — what did they change and why?'
Each student writes one reflection sentence in their notebook: 'The most important thing I learned about making a floating object is _____.' Students share one response aloud to close.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present observations and findings from a design-and-test activity through oral and written expression, connecting their result to the concept tested.
periods.section_context: Oral presentation of boat design decisions; comparison of different groups' boats; strengths and challenges table; reflection on design and floating.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask whether any group's design was inspired by a traditional boat or vessel they had seen or heard of — this creates space for students to share cultural knowledge about water transport without it being imposed.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students list at least two questions Ravi could ask about why a spinner slows down and stops (p. 115)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 115 and read the scenario: Ravi notices his spinner slows down and stops and wants to ask his teacher questions. Teacher asks: 'What would YOU want to know if you saw this happen?'

Students individually write at least two questions Ravi could ask. Teacher prompts those who are stuck: 'Is there something about the spinner itself — its shape, its axle — that might matter? Or is there something about the surface or the air?'

Students share their questions in a circle. Teacher groups similar questions on the board: questions about the spinner's design, questions about forces, questions about materials. Class votes on which question they find most interesting.
Students refine one of their questions to make it testable: 'I would test this by _____.' They write the refined question and their testing idea in their notebooks.

periods.implied_lo: Students can generate and refine inquiry questions about an observed physical phenomenon, distinguishing between questions that can and cannot be tested.
periods.section_context: Ravi's spinner slowing down and stopping; generating inquiry questions; identifying testable questions about spinning behaviour.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students ask questions about why the charkha or lattu eventually stops, welcome them — these are equally valid inquiry questions rooted in familiar objects, and they show students connecting a cultural artefact to the physical phenomenon.

periods.activity_title: Balance and Float: Reasoning and Classification
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students classify objects as float or sink and reason about how to balance a tilting mobile (p. 115–116)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of the tilting mobile (p. 115)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 115 and examine the figure of the hanging mobile bending towards side A. Teacher asks: 'What does 'balance' mean here? What would you need to do to make it level?' Students write a brief response.

Class discusses: what could be added to side B, or removed from side A, to restore balance? Students connect this to the spinner — what happens to a spinner whose axle is off-centre? The concept of balance links both phenomena.

Students open Textbook p. 116 and classify the fourteen objects (wax, marble, thermocol, candle, coin, cork, leaf, eraser, spoon, ice-cube, potato, tomato, pumpkin, lemon) as float or sink in their notebooks. They use their knowledge from earlier in the chapter to reason through any they are unsure of.

Students share their classifications aloud for each object. Where there is disagreement, teacher asks: 'What do you know about this object's shape or material that made you decide?' Students note any changes to their classification after discussion.

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply knowledge of physical properties to classify a range of everyday objects and reason about balance in a simple physical system.
periods.section_context: Tilting mobile figure and balance reasoning; classification of wax, marble, thermocol, candle, coin, cork, leaf, eraser, spoon, ice-cube, potato, tomato, pumpkin, lemon as float or sink.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: For the classification activity, group students so that different regional experiences are represented — students from coastal or riverine areas may have direct experience of some objects (coconut, certain leaves) in water that enriches the group's reasoning.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students reason about changing float/sink behaviour of objects (p. 115)
materials: Small pieces of clay or aluminium foil (optional)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the synthesis by posing two big questions from the chapter's content: 'When does something spin well — and what makes it stop?' and 'When does something float — and what would make it sink?' Students spend a moment writing what they now know about each question.

Students address Textbook p. 115 question: 'How would you make a floating object sink and a sinking object float?' Working individually, they write a response drawing on everything the chapter has explored — shape, material, axle position, weight, design. Teacher circulates and prompts: 'Can you give an example for each direction — floating to sinking, and sinking to floating?'

Whole-class discussion. Students share their strategies for making things float or sink. Teacher connects responses back to the spinning content: 'The spinner works best when balanced at the centre — is there a similar idea of balance in floating?' Students articulate the connecting thread: shape, balance, and the arrangement of material all matter across both phenomena.

Each student writes a closing statement in their notebook: 'The most important thing I would tell someone who wanted to understand how everyday things work is _____.' Several students share their statement aloud. Teacher acknowledges the range of ideas without declaring a single correct answer.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect physical principles from spinning and floating to explain how shape, balance, and material properties govern the behaviour of everyday objects.
periods.section_context: Strategies to make a floating object sink and a sinking object float; connecting spinning/balance and floating/sinking through shape and material properties; chapter-wide reasoning.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Invite students to reflect on whether the charkha, lattu, or traditional boat designs they discussed across the chapter show evidence of understanding these principles — this closing reflection honours both the scientific content and the knowledge embedded in traditional objects.

assessment_items.question_text: Meera says: 'I think the coin, the bangle, and the wooden top will all spin, but the pencil and the eraser will not.' Before she tests them, is this a prediction or a result?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a prediction, because she has not tested the objects yet.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a prediction, but only the wooden top counts because it is made for spinning.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a result, because she has seen these objects before.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a result, because she listed objects that are round.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. The item checks whether students distinguish between a prediction (before testing) and a result (after testing), anchored to the listing-and-predicting activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can generate and refine predictions about which everyday objects are capable of a specified physical behaviour.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student confuses familiarity with an object with having tested it — does not yet distinguish prediction from result.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student uses shape as evidence, conflating a reasonable inference with an actual tested outcome.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student partially grasps 'prediction' but incorrectly limits the concept to objects designed for the activity.

assessment_items.question_text: Arjun spun a coin, a bangle, a pencil, a stone, a wooden top, and an eraser on his desk and recorded what happened. He noticed that the coin and the wooden top spun much better than the others. What two things about those objects might explain why they spun well?
expected_elements: Reference to the shape of the object (round / circular) as a factor that helps spinning.
Reference to the object being balanced or having a point/flat base that keeps it upright during spin.
Any mention of the wooden top having a pointed base or the coin being flat and circular, linked to spinning performance.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for any two distinct, reasoned observations about shape or balance. Award partial credit for one valid point. Do not penalise students for using informal language (e.g., 'it is round all the way around').
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record the physical behaviour of a set of everyday objects under a common test condition.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: The round or circular shape of the coin and wooden top helps them spin.
The wooden top has a pointed base that keeps it stable during spinning; the coin is flat and balanced.
The shape allows the object to stay balanced as it rotates, unlike objects with uneven shapes.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya made two cardboard spinners — in the first, she pushed the toothpick through the centre of the circle; in the second, she pushed it near the edge. She spun both and found that the first spun smoothly while the second wobbled and fell quickly. Give two reasons why the position of the toothpick made a difference.
expected_elements: When the axle is at the centre, the weight of the cardboard is spread evenly around it, so the spinner is balanced.
When the axle is off-centre, one side of the spinner is heavier than the other, causing it to wobble.
A balanced spinner can maintain its rotation; an unbalanced one loses its spin quickly.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for two distinct, reasoned points linking axle position to balance and wobble. Award partial credit for one valid point. Accept informal language.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a hands-on investigation to test how changing the position of a component affects the physical behaviour of a self-made object.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

expected_elements: Centre axle spreads the cardboard's weight evenly, producing a balanced spin.
Off-centre axle means more cardboard on one side, creating imbalance and wobble.
Balance is needed for sustained rotation — without it the spinner falls quickly.

assessment_items.question_text: Deepa made three spinners: one with the hole exactly in the centre, one with the hole slightly off-centre, and one shaped like a square. Which of the following best explains why the square spinner did not spin well?

options.label: A
options.text: The hole in the square spinner was in the centre, which is the wrong position for that shape.

options.label: B
options.text: The square spinner had corners that made its weight uneven as it rotated, so it could not stay balanced.

options.label: C
options.text: The square spinner was made of cardboard, which is too heavy to spin.

options.label: D
options.text: The square spinner was smaller than the other two, so it had less force to keep going.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. The item checks whether students can link shape to balance in a spinner, drawing on the discussion of why spinners fail.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain the effect of a structural variable on the performance of a simple physical device using evidence from their own tests.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student focuses on material weight rather than shape as the variable — has not connected shape to balance.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student confuses the two variables (hole position vs. shape) and applies the centre-hole rule incorrectly to a different variable.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student introduces 'size' as a factor not tested in the activity — suggests over-generalisation from everyday experience.

assessment_items.question_text: Rahul coloured half his spinner disc red and the other half blue. When he spun it slowly, he could see both red and blue clearly. When he spun it very fast, the two colours looked mixed. Which statement best describes what happened?

options.label: A
options.text: The colours mixed because the heat from spinning changed the paint.

options.label: B
options.text: The fast spin removed the colour from the disc, making it look different.

options.label: C
options.text: The prediction was wrong, so the colours must have been applied incorrectly.

options.label: D
options.text: When the disc spun fast, the red and blue parts moved so quickly that the eye saw them blended together.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. The item checks whether students can compare prediction with observation and give a physical reason for the colour-mixing effect during fast rotation.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can make a prediction, carry out a test, and compare the outcome with their prediction to identify whether a physical phenomenon matched their expectation.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.B: Student attributes the visual change to a physical loss of colour rather than to the speed of rotation — conflates a visual effect with a material change.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student introduces a misconception about heat changing paint colour during spinning — not supported by the activity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student misreads 'prediction was wrong' as evidence of an error rather than as a valid inquiry outcome.

assessment_items.question_text: Sonal dropped a leaf, an iron nail, an empty bowl, a stone, and a closed plastic bottle into a bucket of water one at a time. She recorded F (float) or S (sink) for each. She was most surprised by the result for the iron nail and the empty bowl. What did she most likely observe?

options.label: A
options.text: Both the iron nail and the empty bowl floated.

options.label: B
options.text: Both the iron nail and the empty bowl sank.

options.label: C
options.text: The iron nail floated and the empty bowl sank.

options.label: D
options.text: The iron nail sank and the empty bowl floated.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: C. The item checks whether students understand why the bowl (heavy but hollow/shaped) floats and the nail (lighter but dense/narrow) sinks — the key insight that weight alone does not decide the outcome.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record predicted and observed outcomes for a physical test and identify where predictions and results diverge.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student reverses the actual result — may hold a strong weight-based misconception, assigning float to the heavier iron because it is 'metal like a ship'.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Student ignores the nail's density and shape, applying a single rule (metal floats) incorrectly to both objects.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student applies a simple 'heavy objects sink' rule to both without distinguishing shape, missing the bowl's hollow structure.

assessment_items.question_text: Vikram dropped an iron nail and an empty metal bowl into water. The nail sank but the bowl floated. Vikram's friend says: 'That makes no sense — the bowl is heavier than the nail, so it should sink.' Do you agree with Vikram's friend? Write your answer and explain using what you know about floating and sinking.
look_for: Student disagrees with Vikram's friend, showing they understand that weight alone does not determine whether an object floats or sinks.
Student identifies shape or structure as the key additional factor — the bowl's hollow shape traps air or spreads weight differently.
Student supports the explanation with at least one concrete example or comparison from the activity (e.g., the foil in different shapes).
Student's reasoning is logical and connected — not simply asserting 'shape matters' without linking it to the observed outcome.
assessment_items.annotation: Strong responses disagree with the friend and give a shape-based reason for the bowl floating. Partial credit for identifying the disagreement without a clear reason. Do not penalise informal language.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use evidence from a physical test to challenge a simple rule and identify a factor other than the expected one that affects the outcome.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

look_for: Clear disagreement with the friend's statement, with an explicit reason.
Identification of shape (hollow/cup structure) as a factor that allows a heavier object to float.
Connection to the foil experiment or the bowl-vs-nail comparison as evidence.
A logical, connected explanation rather than a list of isolated facts.

assessment_items.question_text: Mira took one sheet of aluminium foil and tested it three times: first spread flat, then pressed into a tight ball, then folded into a cup shape. The flat sheet floated, the ball sank, and the cup floated. What does this tell us about what makes an object float or sink?
expected_elements: The same material can either float or sink depending on its shape.
Shape changes how the object sits in water — a flat or cup shape spreads the object across a larger area, while a ball concentrates the weight in a small space.
The material itself (aluminium foil) is not what decides the outcome — the shape is the deciding factor in this case.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for a response that names shape as the deciding variable and explains why (area or concentration of weight). Award partial credit for correctly identifying that the same material behaved differently without giving a reason.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can investigate how changing the shape of the same material changes its physical behaviour in water and give a reason for the difference.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

expected_elements: The same material (foil) floated in some shapes and sank in others, showing shape — not material alone — determines the outcome.
A flat or cup shape spreads weight over a larger area, helping the object stay on water; a ball concentrates weight in one point.
This means that to make something float, its shape must be considered alongside what it is made of.

assessment_items.task: You have just designed and built a boat. Draw your boat and label the materials you used. Then write two sentences: one about a strength of your boat's design and one about a challenge or something you would change if you built it again.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My boat drawing: [draw here]
Materials I used: _____
One strength of my boat: _____
One thing I would change: _____
format_of_output: A labelled drawing of the boat
A written strength of the design
A written change the student would make
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any boat design. Assess whether the student labels materials, names a genuine strength linked to floating, and identifies a change that shows reflective thinking. Regional note: materials used may vary widely (coconut shells, walnut shells, locally available items) — all are valid and correct.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use local materials to design, build, and evaluate a simple floating object, adjusting the design based on a test result.

competency.competency_text: Uses local materials to create simple objects (family tree, envelopes, origami animals) on their own for display or use in classroom processes

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can connect a design decision to the concept of floating and reflect critically on their own creation.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The drawing shows the boat's shape — check whether the shape reflects an understanding that cup/hollow forms float better. The strength should name a design feature, not just say 'it floated'. The change should be a genuine design improvement, not 'I would make it bigger'.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: labels specific materials; strength names a shape or structural feature; change is specific and linked to a test result. Weak: drawing has no labels; strength is 'it was nice'; change is vague or absent.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students without access to all listed materials may describe or draw a boat using any available materials — coconut shell, folded leaf, or clay are equally valid. Accept oral description if a student cannot draw.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The boat-building activity centred on design and construction; this task asks students to represent and evaluate that product, mirroring the exhibition and comparison the chapter calls for.

assessment_items.task: Think about your boat and one other boat you saw during the class display. Write two sentences comparing them: one way they are similar and one way they are different. Then write one sentence saying which design you think worked better for floating, and why.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My boat used: _____
The other boat used: _____
One way they are similar: _____
One way they are different: _____
I think _____ worked better for floating because: _____
format_of_output: A written similarity between two boats
A written difference between two boats
A written judgement about which design worked better for floating with a reason
assessment_items.annotation: The judgement sentence is the key item — it should connect a design feature (shape, material, size of the base) to floating. Accept any boats for comparison. Regional note: students who describe traditional boat forms (coconut shell, walnut shell boats) are demonstrating valid knowledge — accept and credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present observations and findings from a design-and-test activity through oral and written expression, connecting their result to the concept tested.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can communicate comparative findings in writing and connect a design choice to the concept of floating.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Check that the similarity and difference name actual design features (not just colour or size). The judgement sentence must give a reason linked to floating, not just a preference.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: comparison is specific (e.g., 'both had a wide flat base'; 'mine used clay, theirs used cardboard'); judgement links shape or material to floating performance. Weak: comparison is cosmetic ('both were white'); judgement has no reason.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who could not participate in the exhibition may compare their own boat design to one described in class discussion — this is equally valid.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: This task mirrors the oral presentation and comparison table from the chapter, asking students to consolidate findings in written form as the chapter specifies.

assessment_items.question_text: Ravi's spinner slows down and stops after a while. He wants to ask his teacher a question about this. Which of the following is the BEST inquiry question he could ask?

options.label: A
options.text: Does the surface the spinner spins on affect how long it keeps spinning?

options.label: B
options.text: What colour should I paint my spinner?

options.label: C
options.text: Who invented spinners?

options.label: D
options.text: Why is my spinner made of cardboard?

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. The item checks whether students can identify a testable inquiry question about an observed phenomenon, the key skill developed in the 'Let us reflect' framing activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can generate and refine inquiry questions about an observed physical phenomenon, distinguishing between questions that can and cannot be tested.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.D: Student asks about the material's origin rather than the phenomenon — does not yet see the observation as the starting point for a question.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student asks about an aesthetic property unrelated to the phenomenon — focuses on appearance rather than behaviour.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Student asks a historical question rather than an investigable one — does not connect the observed slowing to a testable variable.

assessment_items.question_text:
Look at the list below. Sort these objects into two groups — those that float in water and those that sink. Objects: wax, marble, thermocol, candle, coin, cork, leaf, eraser, spoon, ice-cube, potato, tomato, pumpkin, lemon. Write each object in the correct column.

| Floats | Sinks |
|--------|-------|
expected_elements: Floats column should include: wax, thermocol, cork, leaf, ice-cube, pumpkin, candle, lemon (and tomato — borderline; accept in either column with reasoning).
Sinks column should include: marble, coin, eraser, spoon, potato (and tomato — borderline; accept in either column with reasoning).
Student has placed the majority of objects in the correct column, showing they can apply float/sink knowledge to unfamiliar objects.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept tomato and lemon in either column — they are borderline in fresh water and may genuinely float or sink depending on ripeness. Regional note: students with direct experience of placing vegetables and fruits in water (e.g., during cooking or play) may have valid experiential knowledge that differs slightly from textbook lists — credit reasoning alongside placement.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply knowledge of physical properties to classify a range of everyday objects and reason about balance in a simple physical system.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

expected_elements: Majority of objects correctly classified based on density and shape knowledge built across the chapter.
Borderline cases (tomato, lemon) accepted in either column if a reason is given.
Classification reflects application of the float/sink concept to new objects, not just recall of tested items.

assessment_items.question_text: Think about everything you have explored in this chapter — spinning objects, making spinners, testing what floats and sinks, and building boats. Choose ONE thing you learned that surprised you. Explain what surprised you and why, using examples from the chapter.
look_for: Student identifies a specific finding from the chapter (not a general statement like 'I learned a lot').
Student explains WHY it was surprising — what they had expected before, and how the result differed.
Student uses at least one concrete example from the chapter's content (a specific object, shape, or test).
Student connects the surprising finding to a broader principle — about shape, balance, or material — even informally.
assessment_items.annotation: This item synthesises the whole chapter. There is no single correct answer — credit the quality of reasoning and the use of a specific example. Strong responses name a precise finding, contrast it with a prior expectation, and connect it to the chapter's underlying ideas. Do not penalise students who choose examples from spinning rather than floating, or vice versa.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect physical principles from spinning and floating to explain how shape, balance, and material properties govern the behaviour of everyday objects.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

look_for: A specific, named finding from the chapter — not a vague reference to 'what I learned'.
A clear before/after contrast: what the student expected vs. what they found.
A concrete example (e.g., the foil ball sinking while the foil cup floated; the off-centre spinner wobbling; the heavy bowl floating).
An informal but recognisable link to a physical principle — shape matters, balance matters, material alone does not decide.
